candidates.name: Steve Hilton
candidates.bio_short: Fox News contributor; former host of The Next Revolution (2017–2023); former senior adviser to UK PM David Cameron. Endorsed by Donald Trump (2026-04-06).
candidates.money_raised_note: $6.6M cumulative per April 2026 reporting; CalMatters H2-2025 filing showed $4.1M.

bio.race_ethnicity: White; British-American of Hungarian descent (parents emigrated from Hungary during the 1956 revolution); self-identifies as immigrant son. Naturalized U.S. citizen May 11, 2021.
bio.net_worth_note: No public net-worth estimate; CalMatters (March 2026) reports $7.5M joint 2024 income with wife Rachel Whetstone (Netflix CCO) — $250K from Fox News, $6.7M from wife's Netflix role, $360K from global investments, $25K from three London rental properties. Independent estimates range $3-10M (uncited tabloids).
bio.self_funded_note: Not a major self-funder; raised >$6.6M from donors as of April 2026 per Wikipedia/Ballotpedia. Wealthy by income but not self-funding at Steyer scale.
bio.education: BA Philosophy, Politics and Economics — New College, Oxford (1991)

bio_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hilton — DOB, birthplace, education, career history, naturalization date, marriage
candidates.bio_notes: Hilton resides in Atherton/Silicon Valley; classified as bay_area for residence. No public net worth estimate from a credible source — left null. Religion not publicly discussed; left 'not publicly stated'. Electability score of 5 reflects SurveyUSA May 1, 2026 lead at 20%.

candidates.name: Tom Steyer
candidates.bio_short: Billionaire investor, environmental activist, and 2020 presidential candidate; founder of Farallon Capital and NextGen America. Campaign is largely self-funded.
candidates.money_raised_note: Largely self-funded through April 2026 per CapRadio. On track for most expensive gubernatorial campaign in CA history.

bio.birthplace: Manhattan, New York City, New York
bio.race_ethnicity: White; Jewish father (Roy Henry Steyer, Nuremberg prosecutor) and Episcopalian mother. Steyer identifies as Episcopalian Christian (converted/embraced in his late 30s).
bio.net_worth_note: Forbes April 2026 estimate: $2.4 billion. Founded Farallon Capital (1986), left 2012. Signed The Giving Pledge.
bio.self_funded_note: As of late April 2026, ~$122.5M of $122.7M raised was self-funded (~99.9%). Total campaign spend on track to exceed $147M, approaching Meg Whitman's 2010 state record (~$144M self-funded of $176M).
bio.education: MBA — Stanford Graduate School of Business (1983). BA in economics and political science (summa cum laude) — Yale University (1979).

bio_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Steyer — DOB, education, career, family, net worth
candidates.bio_notes: Self-identifies as Episcopalian Christian; some sources note Jewish paternal heritage. Both demographic tags applied. Resides in San Francisco. Electability 5 anchored on 18% SurveyUSA (May 1), strong fundraising, and labor/environmental endorsements.

issues.name: Housing supply & zoning preemption
issues.short_description: How aggressively should the state push to build more housing, including over local objection?
issues.ca_specific_context: Local control under CEQA and city zoning has historically blocked dense infill; recent state law (SB 9, SB 10, SB 423) preempts some of that.

stance_scale.label: Build aggressively — preempt local zoning where it blocks supply
Build a lot — strong state targets, modest preemption
Build with balance — state nudges, local control preserved
Slow growth — protect neighborhood character and existing residents
Focus on subsidies and tenant protections, not supply

issues.name: Homelessness response
issues.short_description: Where should the state's approach to homelessness sit on the enforcement-to-services spectrum?
issues.ca_specific_context: Prop 1 (2024) expanded conservatorship and mental-health funding; cities differ widely on encampment sweeps; SB 43 widened the bar for conservatorship.

stance_scale.label: Aggressive clearance — sweeps and expanded conservatorship as primary tools
Enforcement-first with concurrent service offers
Balanced — enforcement only when shelter/services are available
Housing-first primarily, minimal enforcement
Heavy investment in supportive housing and services; treat enforcement as last resort

issues.name: Middle-income tax rates
issues.short_description: Where should state income tax rates for middle-income earners go?
issues.ca_specific_context: California's progressive income tax has top marginal rate ~13.3%; middle brackets fund the bulk of state services.

stance_scale.label: Significantly cut middle-income tax rates
Modestly cut middle-income rates
Hold current rates
Modestly raise middle-income rates
Significantly raise middle-income rates

issues.name: Top-bracket / corporate / wealth tax
issues.short_description: Should CA raise taxes on top earners, corporations, or introduce a wealth tax?
issues.ca_specific_context: Multiple wealth-tax bills (e.g., AB 259) have been proposed; corporate tax is 8.84%.

stance_scale.label: Cut top-bracket and corporate rates
Hold current top rates
Modestly raise top-bracket and/or corporate rates
Substantially raise top-bracket and corporate rates
Introduce a new state-level wealth tax on highest earners

issues.name: Commercial property tax (Prop 13 split-roll)
issues.short_description: Should commercial property be taxed at market value (split-roll), or stay under Prop 13?
issues.ca_specific_context: Prop 15 (2020) would have implemented a commercial split-roll; failed 52-48.

stance_scale.label: Strengthen Prop 13 protections for commercial property
Hold Prop 13 protections for commercial property
Targeted reforms (e.g., apply only to very large commercial holdings)
Phase in commercial split-roll
Full commercial split-roll — tax commercial at market value

issues.name: Residential Prop 13 protections
issues.short_description: Should residential Prop 13 protections be preserved, narrowed, or rolled back?
issues.ca_specific_context: Prop 13 (1978) caps property tax at 1% of assessed value with limited increases; Prop 19 (2020) restricted parent-child transfers.

stance_scale.label: Strengthen residential Prop 13 protections
Hold current residential protections
Limited reforms (e.g., transfer-rule tweaks)
Significant reforms while preserving primary-home protection
Phase out residential Prop 13

issues.name: Utility rate regulation
issues.short_description: What role should the state play in setting electricity, gas, and insurance rates?
issues.ca_specific_context: PG&E, SCE, SDG&E rates have risen sharply; CPUC reform and proposals to replace investor-owned utilities are active debate.

stance_scale.label: Deregulate — let market and competition set rates
Modest regulation, focus on grid investment
Rate freeze and significant CPUC reform
Public option / break up monopolies
Full state takeover of investor-owned utilities

issues.name: California gas excise tax
issues.short_description: Should CA's gas excise tax be suspended, held, or expanded?
issues.ca_specific_context: SB 1 (2017) raised the tax and earmarked revenue for transportation; current rate among highest in US.

stance_scale.label: Suspend the gas excise tax
Pause scheduled increases
Hold the current rate
Modestly raise the tax for transportation investment
Significantly raise the tax, earmark for climate / transit

issues.name: Fuel and refinery environmental rules
issues.short_description: Should LCFS, refinery emissions rules, and related fuel mandates be loosened, held, or tightened?
issues.ca_specific_context: Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) and CARB rules push refineries toward lower-carbon fuels; oil industry argues this raises pump prices.

stance_scale.label: Suspend LCFS and refinery environmental rules
Weaken specific rules to lower gas prices
Maintain current rules
Tighten specific rules to accelerate decarbonization
Major expansion of fuel emissions regulation

issues.name: Policing and criminal penalties
issues.short_description: What's the right balance between expanding police capacity, reform, and non-police alternatives?
issues.ca_specific_context: Fentanyl deaths, retail-theft enforcement, and police oversight debates have all driven CA policy since 2024.

stance_scale.label: Significantly expand law enforcement and toughen penalties

Mixed approach — more officers AND more accountability/diversion

issues.name: Prop 36 / Prop 47 direction
issues.short_description: Should CA go further on rolling back Prop 47, hold Prop 36 as passed, or restore Prop 47?
issues.ca_specific_context: Prop 47 (2014) reduced certain felonies to misdemeanors; Prop 36 (2024) rolled back parts of that; implementation is still in progress.

stance_scale.label: Go further than Prop 36 — significantly toughen penalties
Implement Prop 36 fully, consider further toughening
Implement Prop 36 as passed; no further changes
Implement narrowly; advocate restoring some Prop 47 protections
Restore Prop 47 in full; expand diversion programs

issues.name: Sanctuary and immigration enforcement
issues.short_description: What should CA's posture be on cooperation with federal immigration enforcement?
issues.ca_specific_context: SB 54 (2017) limits state cooperation with ICE; under renewed federal pressure as of 2025–2026.

stance_scale.label: Repeal SB 54; full ICE cooperation
Allow specific exceptions to SB 54
Maintain SB 54 as-is

issues.name: Water storage and conveyance projects

issues.ca_specific_context: CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act) is widely blamed for project delays; multiple targeted reform bills (e.g., AB 1633, SB 423) have passed since 2023.

issues.name: School choice and charters

issues.ca_specific_context: AB 1505 (2019) gave districts more charter denial authority; vouchers have repeatedly failed at the ballot.

options.label: Major California newspapers (LA Times, SF Chronicle, Sac Bee)

positions.summary: Hilton wants more homes but emphatically opposes state preemption of local zoning, framing SB 79 and Sacramento densification mandates as a threat to single-family neighborhoods. His supply strategy is deregulatory (cap impact fees, gut CEQA, defang the Coastal Commission and CARB) rather than upzoning.
positions.source_quote: Republican Steve Hilton warned that SB 79 will 'destroy' California's 'single-family suburban neighborhoods' by allowing the construction of mid-rise apartment buildings. The former Fox News host objects to state-led planning mandates and to the prevailing orthodoxy among YIMBY-aligned Democrats in Sacramento that the state should focus new construction in dense urban areas.
positions.notes: Stance 4 (slow growth / protect neighborhood character) is the best fit because while Hilton talks about building more, he opposes the main tool the state has to actually preempt the local 'no' (SB 79) and frames the issue as defending suburbs. His own site uses 'war on single family homes' and 'Restore the California Dream of a single family home for every family.'

positions.summary: Steyer pledged to build one million homes in four years and was one of two leading Democrats (with Porter) who publicly championed SB 79 during the legislative fight, not just after signing. He explicitly endorses state intervention when localities block housing.
positions.source_quote: The state has passed critical laws to streamline permitting, increase density, and prioritize housing near transit, which I championed (SB 79) and helped lobby to pass... if local governments refuse to follow the law and seek to block housing, the state will step in.
positions.notes: California YIMBY characterizes Steyer as 'a vocal, public supporter of SB 79 throughout the legislative fight,' showing up when it was politically costly. The 'one million homes over four years' number comes directly from his housing plan page.

positions.summary: Bianco's housing platform is pure deregulation: eliminate CEQA, expedite permits, incentivize builders, and defend Prop 13. He has not endorsed state preemption of local zoning, and California YIMBY says he has 'said little on housing other than blaming his political opponents.'
positions.source_quote: Expedite approval for housing projects... Eliminate CEQA and the litigation that only passes costs onto the homebuyer... End the over regulation of our building industry... Incentivize developers to build across California.
positions.notes: Stance 3 ('build with balance, local control preserved') is the best available fit: he wants more supply via deregulation but is silent on state zoning preemption and defends Prop 13/local primacy. His housing page is thin and CalMatters did not document a position from him on SB 79.

positions.summary: Becerra would treat housing as essential infrastructure, declare a housing state of emergency on day one, and expand SB 79 and SB 684 to end exclusionary zoning beyond transit areas. He explicitly says communities should have a voice but 'not a veto.'
positions.source_quote: Last year's SB 79 created the zoning for more housing, especially affordable housing, near rail transit... Communities should have a voice in this process but they should not have a veto over the obligation.
positions.notes: Becerra's platform language is explicitly preemption-friendly ('not a veto'), pushing stance toward 1. California YIMBY notes he came to housing late as a campaign priority and only endorsed SB 79 after Newsom signed it, so he's slightly less proven on the fight than Steyer/Porter, but his published platform is firmly in the aggressive-preemption camp.

positions.summary: Porter publicly backed SB 79 during the legislative fight (including breaking with skilled-labor language) and centers her housing plan on shaving two years off construction timelines and bringing apartment costs down 20%, including by stopping local delays after entitlement.
positions.source_quote: I disagree on SB79. I support it and was glad to see @CA_Dem endorse it this weekend. Workers, students, seniors and other Californians will all benefit from more housing—especially near transit.
positions.notes: Porter is grouped with Steyer as one of the two Dems who publicly supported SB 79 'when it mattered.' Her own site emphasizes supply acceleration ('speed up building by nearly two years', 'stopping local delays that too often occur even after the projects receive a building entitlement'). The tweet date is approximated to August 2025 around when CA Dems endorsed SB 79; URL is verbatim from the search result.

positions.summary: Mahan has the strongest production track record of any candidate — his San Jose fee reform turned zero market-rate starts into ~2,000 ground-breakings — and supports deregulation, capped local fees, and code reform. But he conspicuously did not endorse SB 79 and previously opposed SB 9, making him noticeably more cautious on outright state zoning preemption than Steyer/Porter/Becerra.
positions.source_quote: As Mayor, Matt Mahan cut excessive regulation and red tape – as a result, San Jose has built new homes for the first time in years and lowered housing costs.
positions.notes: Despite the YIMBY-friendly press, California YIMBY explicitly observes: 'Mayor Mahan didn't endorse SB 79, and stopped shy of calling out zoning as the problem almost every time.' He opposed SB 9. That puts him at 2 (strong state targets and supply push, but modest rather than aggressive preemption of local zoning), not 1.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa pairs CEQA modernization, streamlined permits, and a Housing Production Accountability Board to enforce RHNA targets with a $25B revenue-bond Middle-Class Homeownership Act aimed at financing 100,000–150,000 new middle-income homes. Heavy on supply and accountability, but with less explicit endorsement of zoning preemption than Becerra/Steyer/Porter.
positions.source_quote: Reforming CEQA, streamlining permits, and enforcing production accountability can close the gap between planning and building... As a temporary situation, I'm for [rent control]... if you want to bring down rents over the long term, you need supply.
positions.notes: Stance 2 (strong state targets, modest preemption) fits: his plan emphasizes RHNA enforcement and supply, but the policy levers are CEQA/permit reform and homebuyer financing rather than an explicit SB 79-style upzoning posture. The second clause of the quote is from his CalMatters interview confirming a supply-first long-run framing.

positions.summary: Thurmond's housing pitch is built around a $10B affordable-housing bond, building up to 2 million subsidized units on surplus school-district land, down-payment assistance, and taxing corporate housing speculators. He has not articulated a position on SB 79 or local-zoning preemption.
positions.source_quote: California has 2.3 million housing units hiding in plain sight on surplus school district land sitting vacant across the state. I'm working with our top housing leaders to give school districts the startup funding they need to develop that land building homes for teachers...
positions.notes: Stance 5 (focus on subsidies and tenant-side policy rather than market supply) is the closest fit: every concrete plank is a subsidy, public-land, bond, or anti-speculator measure rather than a deregulatory or preemption lever. He hasn't taken a public SB 79 position. Stance could arguably be 3 because the school-land plan is supply-additive, but the bias is clearly subsidy-led, not preemption-led.

positions.summary: Hilton's primary lever is law enforcement: clear encampments first under Grants Pass authority, then triage. He calls Housing First a 'complete disaster' and would redirect funding to 'sober housing' with sobriety conditions, framing the status quo as a $24 billion 'catastrophic failure.'
positions.source_quote: This is against the law, and the law needs to be enforced. [Hilton] called the existing 'housing first' philosophy a 'complete disaster' and instead wants to free up all state funding to support sober housing.
positions.notes: Stance 1 (aggressive clearance) fits because removal-first is his explicit sequencing. He ducked specifics on conservatorship standards when pressed by CalMatters, so he's not as fully committed to expanded involuntary commitment as Bianco — but his enforcement-first framing and rejection of Housing First put him at the most aggressive end of the scale.

positions.summary: Steyer is 'fully committed to a Housing First approach' but pairs it with 'bridge housing with robust stabilization services' and a spending review — he treats homelessness as primarily a housing-supply and care-matching problem, not an enforcement problem. He has not endorsed sweeps or expanded conservatorship.
positions.source_quote: No one gets better on the street... [Steyer is] fully committed to a Housing First approach... matching the right housing with the right level of care.
positions.notes: Stance 4 rather than 5 because his framing leans heavily on bridge/interim housing as the urgent immediate step (a moderate position) and he wants a 'full spending review' — not a stance 5 'pour more money in' posture. He has not addressed encampment sweeps or conservatorship directly in his public platform, which lowers confidence.

positions.summary: Bianco wants the state to use Grants Pass to clear encampments, force people into treatment via new legislation, and cut off all nonprofit/HHAP funding. He rejects the 'homeless' framing entirely and claims ~95% of people on the street are addicted — the most enforcement-and-treatment-coercive platform in the field.
positions.source_quote: This is not about homes. Stop calling it homeless... We have to get to a point where the Legislature passes a law that we can actually force people into mental health treatment... No NGO and no nonprofit is going to get money with me as the governor.
positions.notes: Stance 1 is the unambiguous fit: he explicitly wants forced treatment legislation beyond what SB 43 and Prop 1 already allow, and would zero out nonprofit homelessness funding. His own platform page lists Grants Pass-based encampment clearance as Pillar 1.

positions.summary: Becerra explicitly endorses Housing First 'always paired, where needed, with behavioral health and addiction treatment,' commits to implementing every Prop 1 reform, and frames shelter as 'a bridge, not an endpoint.' His main innovation is accountability dashboards and tying HHAP funding to outcomes, not enforcement.
positions.source_quote: Housing First approaches, always paired, where needed, with behavioral health and addiction treatment... This is not a housing crisis alone. It is a mental health crisis... expand shelter capacity as a bridge, not an endpoint.
positions.notes: Stance 4 rather than 5 because his Prop 1 / conservatorship enthusiasm and his 'communities that fail will face real consequences' framing carry meaningful coercive edges — he isn't a pure services-only candidate. He declined to participate in the Press Democrat round-up, and his campaign page is the cleanest articulation.

positions.summary: Porter frames homelessness as 'a direct correlate of our housing problems' and emphasizes prevention (emergency rental assistance, rapid re-housing) plus interim housing as 'absolutely necessary.' She has not endorsed sweeps or expanded conservatorship and treats unsheltered status itself as a mental-health/substance-use risk factor.
positions.source_quote: It is so much more cost-effective and so much more humane to prevent families from becoming homeless in the first place... [her plan focuses on] homeless prevention through emergency rental assistance and rapid re-housing, and interim housing that can keep people from being unsheltered, which is itself a risk factor for mental health and substance use problems.
positions.notes: Stance 4 fits her prevention-and-housing-supply emphasis. Confidence is medium because she has not publicly addressed CARE Court, SB 43, or sweeps in detail — a notable gap given how prominent those debates are. If she were to articulate them, she could easily move to stance 5.

positions.summary: Mahan describes an 'all-of-the-above' approach and 'mass treatment' on his gubernatorial campaign — but his actual San Jose record is the most enforcement-forward of any Democrat in the field: his June 2025 'Responsibility to Shelter' ordinance lets the city cite and ultimately arrest unhoused people who refuse three shelter offers in 18 months. He also openly endorses 30-60 day involuntary commitment as 'a temporary suspension of certain civil liberties.'
positions.source_quote: I don't think it's humane or compassionate to allow people to live or die on our streets when they are unable or unwilling to accept the help the city is able to offer... The compassionate thing to do is to intervene. And yes, that may look like a temporary suspension of certain civil liberties.
positions.notes: GOVERNANCE-RHETORIC GAP. Mahan's gubernatorial site ('balancing compassion with accountability,' 'mass treatment not mass incarceration') reads like a stance 3. But his actual San Jose ordinance — citation on first two refusals, arrest on the third within 18 months, with explicit intent to use arrests to compel court-ordered treatment — is materially more coercive than any other Democrat in this field. Coding to the record (stance 2: enforcement-first with concurrent service offers), not the rhetoric. Santa Clara County's DA and Sheriff publicly opposed the ordinance.

positions.summary: Villaraigosa rejects criminalization ('I'm not for criminalizing homelessness. I am for compassion. But I'm not for chaos') and prioritizes housing construction (including tiny homes), but he also wants to convene experts to lower the bar for locked psychiatric conservatorship and would withhold HHAP funding from counties that underperform on CARE Court.
positions.source_quote: I'm not for criminalizing homeless(ness). I am for compassion. But I'm not for chaos... sometimes the compassionate course of action is to commit them to a locked psychiatric institution.
positions.notes: Stance 3 is the best fit because he pairs a clear anti-criminalization line with a willingness to expand involuntary commitment for severe mental illness and to use HHAP funding as a stick. The 'compassion vs chaos' framing is his deliberate middle position. His current campaign site does not foreground homelessness positions — most detail comes from the CalMatters interview.

positions.summary: Thurmond's platform is build-and-treat: 2 million affordable units on surplus school land by 2030, a $10B housing bond including tiny homes, taxing the wealthy to fund mental-health services, and conditioning housing-program participation on treatment 'if applicable.' He has not endorsed sweeps or expanded conservatorship.
positions.source_quote: [Thurmond] favors taxing the state's wealthiest residents more to pay for health care, including mental health services for those experiencing or at risk of homelessness, and he supports housing programs that require participants to undergo treatment if applicable to their situation.
positions.notes: Stance 4 fits his housing-supply-plus-services emphasis. Confidence is medium because his campaign site lacks a dedicated homelessness page — positions are reconstructed from CapRadio and Press Democrat reporting. The 'treatment if applicable' condition keeps him from a pure stance 5; he has not endorsed any specific encampment-enforcement or conservatorship-expansion position.
